title: Design a demand forecasting system for a grocery chain with 2,000 stores
prompt:
**Interviewer:** A grocery chain has **2,000 stores** and about **30,000 SKUs** (products). On average **35%** of the store-SKU pairs are active. Stores place orders **every night at 22:00**; trucks arrive **2 days later**. About **20%** of SKUs are fresh food with 3 to 5 days of shelf life. The chain has 3 years of daily sales, price, promotion and inventory data. Planners today use last year's sales plus a manual uplift. Waste costs the chain about 2 times the margin of an item; for non-fresh items a stock-out costs about 1 time the margin.

Design a forecasting system that produces **daily forecasts for the next 14 days per store and SKU** and supports the ordering decision. Think about data, models, evaluation, serving, and what can go wrong.

sections.label: Requirements & decision
sections.hint: Who orders? Which horizon do you really need (lead time + review)? Fresh vs non-fresh costs? Point or quantile forecast?

sections.label: Data & features
sections.hint: Sales vs demand, stock-outs, price, promotions, calendar, weather, new items. Which features are known in advance?

sections.label: Models & baselines
sections.hint: Baseline first. Global or local? How to handle intermittent and new items? Quantiles?

sections.label: Evaluation & backtest
sections.hint: Rolling origin, metric choice, segments, FVA vs the planners' current method, business cost.

sections.label: Serving & scale
sections.hint: Number of series, nightly window, batch vs online, storage, fallbacks, cost.

sections.label: Monitoring & failure modes
sections.hint: Bias alerts, drift, label delay, retraining, promotions that were not entered, feedback with the planners.

model_answer.req:
**Decision.** Each night a store orders quantity per SKU. The order arrives in 2 days, so the order must cover demand from day 2 until the next delivery. If trucks come every day, the protection period is lead time (2) + review period (1) = **3 days**, so I need accurate forecasts for days 2 to 4 above all. A 14-day horizon is still useful for planning shifts, promotions and supplier contracts, but accuracy at day 2-4 drives waste and stock-outs.

**Cost of errors.** Fresh items: waste costs about 2× margin, stock-out about 1× margin, so cu/(cu+co) = 1/3: order the **33rd percentile** of demand. Non-fresh items: costs are about equal on the margin side, but a stock-out also loses the customer trip, so I would use a **60-70th percentile** (to confirm with the business). So I need **quantile forecasts**, not only the mean.

**Size.** 2,000 × 30,000 × 0.35 = **21 million active series**, 14 values each = about 294 million forecast rows per night. Nightly window: from final sales (about 21:00) to 22:00 orders, so roughly **1 hour** to compute.

**Success.** Lower waste and fewer stock-outs than the current method, measured by FVA against last-year-plus-uplift and a seasonal naive.
model_answer.data:
**Sources.** Daily sales per store-SKU, price, promotion calendar (planned, with type and depth), store attributes, SKU hierarchy (category, brand, shelf life), holiday and event calendar, weather forecast for the region, inventory and delivery data.

**Sales are not demand.** On stock-out days sales are capped. I mark days with zero stock or very low availability as censored, and use availability as a feature. For the model, I can drop these targets or train with a censored objective. I will report the share of stock-out days.

**Features known at order time (point-in-time):** lags (7, 14, 28, 365 days) and rolling means of sales **ending at the order time**; day of week, day of month, holidays and days to/from holiday; price, price change vs last 28 days, promotion flags and depth, **planned** values for the future days; store and SKU ids/categories; weather forecast as it was available that night.

**Leakage guard.** Feature store with timestamps and point-in-time joins. Future promotions are allowed only if they were entered before the order time.

**Hard cases.** New items (no history): use hierarchy features (category, price band) and the history of similar items. Substitution: a stock-out of a close substitute lifts the sales of this item. Returns and data corrections arrive late.
model_answer.model:
**Baselines.** Seasonal naive (same weekday last week) and the planners' method (last year + uplift). These set the bar and are the fallback.

**Main model.** A **global gradient-boosting model** (LightGBM style) trained on all series together, with lag, calendar, price, promotion and hierarchy features. Reasons: handles 21M series with one training job, learns from similar items, deals with new items via features, strong results in public competitions such as M5. I would train **one model per horizon bucket** (days 1-3, 4-7, 8-14) or a direct multi-horizon model, and **quantile objectives** (for example 0.33, 0.5, 0.7, 0.9) instead of one mean model. Fresh and non-fresh items may use different quantile levels.

**Slow and intermittent items.** Many SKUs sell 0-2 units per store per day. Use a count-based loss (Tweedie or Poisson) and forecast at store-group level then allocate, or use a simple rate-based method (Croston-like) as a candidate.

**Promotions.** Promotion effect is big. Include depth, type and a 'last promo' history. Allow planners to override for rare events, and measure the FVA of the overrides.

**Later.** Hierarchical reconciliation so store forecasts add up to region and national numbers; deep global models only if the gain is proven.
model_answer.eval:
**Backtest.** Rolling origin: 8 to 12 recent weekly origins, each trained on data before the origin and tested on the following 14 days. Include a holiday period and a promotion-heavy period. No random split.

**Metrics.** **WAPE** and **bias** per segment (fresh/non-fresh, volume class, region), because MAPE breaks on small values. **Pinball loss** at the ordering quantile. For the decision: simulate the ordering policy with the forecast and compute **waste and stock-out cost** (a replay or 'what-if' simulation), because the business pays for cost, not for WAPE.

**FVA.** Compare each step: seasonal naive, planners' method, model, model + manual override. Report FVA per segment.

**Fairness to stock-outs.** Evaluate on non-censored days, and also report results on all days with a flag.

**Acceptance rule.** Roll out store by store (A/B test: matched stores or time-based switch-back) and compare waste and availability, not only accuracy.
model_answer.serve:
**Pattern.** Nightly **batch** job: ingest final sales, validate, build features (feature store, point-in-time), predict quantiles, write to a table keyed by (date, store, sku, horizon) by **upsert**, publish to the ordering system. No online serving needed for orders.

**Compute estimate.** 21M series. A global tree model predicting 14 horizons × 4 quantiles is about 1.2 billion predictions. With a vectorised tree model at roughly 1-2 million predictions per second per core, 64 cores handle this in about **10-20 minutes**. Feature building is the bigger cost, so I compute lags with a partitioned DataFrame job (partition by store). Training weekly takes a few hours, off the critical path.

**Storage.** 294M rows/night × 4 quantiles. Keep 90 days of forecasts for accuracy tracking (about 26 billion rows at row level; compress as columnar files, partitioned by date) and keep older data at aggregated level.

**Reliability.** Partition by store so a failure affects one store. Fallback chain: model forecast, seasonal naive, last order. Sanity limits per item (for example forecast ≤ 5× the 8-week maximum, no negatives). Idempotent jobs so a retry or backfill is safe. A partial run publishes the successful stores and alerts for the rest.

**Cost.** Track compute minutes per run and cost per forecast, and review it each month.
model_answer.monitor:
**Layers.** (1) Data quality: file arrival, row counts per store, missing days, price/promotion feed completeness. (2) Input drift: PSI on top features, share of items with no history. (3) Forecast error: WAPE, bias and tracking signal per segment as actuals arrive (label delay: 1 day), compared with seasonal naive. (4) Business: waste and availability.

**Failure modes.** Promotion not entered in the system, so sales jump and the model is surprised. New store opening, store closure for remodeling, a supplier problem that creates stock-outs (censored data), a price-feed bug (price 0), a holiday shift (Easter), a weather extreme, a COVID-like shock (concept drift).

**Retraining.** Weekly time-based retrain; extra retrain if bias tracking signal passes 4 for a segment or PSI > 0.25 on key features. New models run as challengers in shadow mode for 2 weeks and are promoted only if they win the backtest and the shadow comparison.

**Humans.** Planners can override with a reason code. We track FVA of overrides and show where the model is weak. Alerts go to an owner with a runbook.

**Feedback loops.** If the forecast changes stock, which changes sales data, keep availability as a feature and log the forecast used for each order.

rubric.item: Starts from the ordering decision, lead time and protection period before naming a model
Asks about or derives cost of errors and uses a quantile (newsvendor) target, not only the mean
Sizes the problem with numbers (series count, rows per night, compute time)
Explains that sales are censored demand and handles stock-outs
Uses point-in-time features and states which features are known in advance (planned price, promotions)
Proposes a baseline and a global model, with a plan for new and intermittent items
Uses a rolling-origin backtest, WAPE/bias/pinball, FVA, and a business-cost replay
Designs batch serving with idempotent jobs, fallbacks and partial success
Monitors data quality, drift, bias and business metrics, with a retraining and challenger plan
Mentions human overrides, feedback loops and rollout by A/B test

follow_ups: A new store opens tomorrow. What forecast do you use for the first 4 weeks?
Planners override your forecast 40% of the time and say the model is wrong at Easter. What do you do?
A supplier problem causes empty shelves for 10 days in one region. How does it affect training, and what do you change?
The business wants one number per store per day for staffing as well. How do you make store totals and SKU forecasts consistent?
How would your design change for a food-delivery app that needs forecasts per zone every 15 minutes?
Compute cost doubled this month. How do you find why and what do you cut first?
